skill.name: Read it back: find what doesn't make sense
skill.why: Writers miss their own slips. Reading it back catches them before readers do.
skill.how: Read slowly, one sentence at a time. Ask: does this make sense with the rest?

steps.say: Here's Mo's cake review. Every sentence sounds fine. So first, I find the fact the rest must fit.

show.text: Tully cracked a tooth on it.
show.nudge: That's what happened to Tully. Which sentence says what the cake is like?

show.text: Gus used a slice as a doorstop.
show.nudge: That's what Gus did with it. Which sentence says what the cake itself is like?

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that says what the cake is like.
steps.win: Yes! Rock hard is the key fact. Every other sentence has to fit it.

steps.say: Mo added one more line. Now I check every sentence against rock hard.

show.nudge: That's the key fact. Check the other sentences against it.
A rock hard cake could crack a tooth. That fits.

show.text: Gus used it as a doorstop.
show.nudge: A rock hard cake could hold a door open. That fits.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that doesn't fit the key fact.
steps.win: Yes! Melting doesn't fit rock hard. Two sentences that can't both be true make a clash.

steps.say: Zed read the draft and said every sentence was fine. Each one does sound fine alone!
steps.ask: So why did Zed miss the slip?

options.text: He read each sentence alone, not against the key fact.
He skipped the last sentence.
options.reason: He read them all. What didn't he check each sentence against?

options.text: A word is missing from it.
options.reason: Read it aloud. No word is missing. The problem is how it fits with the rest.

steps.win: Yes! Slips hide between sentences. Always check each one against the key fact.

steps.say: Some slips are smaller. I read aloud, slowly, the way I'd say it. Listen.

show.text: Gran the scones in the oven.

options.text: hot
options.reason: Say it: 'Gran hot the scones.' What did Gran do? You need a doing word.

options.text: put
and
options.reason: 'Gran and the scones in the oven'? Now Gran is in the oven too! What did she do?

steps.win: Yes! Gran put the scones in the oven. Reading aloud helps you hear the gap.

steps.say: Jumbled words can flip who does what. Read each one and picture it.

show.nudge: Picture it. Mo can catch a fish. That makes sense.

show.text: The fish was caught by Mo.
show.nudge: Read it slowly. Who caught the fish? Mo did. That makes sense.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that doesn't make sense.
steps.win: Yes! A fish can't catch Mo. The words got jumbled, so the meaning flipped.

steps.say: Zed wants to fix 'The fish was caught by Mo', because Mo comes last.

show.text: The fish was caught by Mo.

check.nudge: Read it again. Do you know who caught what? If it makes sense, it's fine.

steps.win: Right! It makes sense, so leave it. Mo can come last. Only fix what doesn't make sense.

encounters.frame: Gus's report on rumbling stomachs is going in the science page. The Nodrake's tummy is rumbling too.
encounters.text: Your stomach muscles squeeze all day long, mixing food and pushing it along into your gut. When your stomach is full, the food muffles that squeezing, so you hardly hear a thing. When it is empty, only gas and juices are left sloshing around, and the squeezing echoes like a drum. The rumble is loudest right after a big meal, when your stomach is completely empty. So a loud growl is really your body's way of announcing that it's snack time.
